Mite
MITE
n.
From Middle Dutch mite, “a small coin”; renders the Greek lepton, “a thin one,” the smallest copper coin in circulation in NT-era Palestine, worth about 1/128 of a denarius (a single day’s wage for a laborer).

📖 Biblical Definition

The mite was the smallest copper coin in circulation in the first-century Roman East, rendering the Greek lepton (literally a thin one, the lightest and least-valuable of coins). Two mites made a kodrantes (quadrans, a small Roman copper); 128 quadrantes made a denarius (a single day’s wage); so the mite was worth approximately 1/256 of a day’s wage—the smallest currency unit in actual circulation. The word’s supreme biblical use is the parable-narrative of the widow’s mites in Mark 12:41-44 and Luke 21:1-4. Christ is sitting in the temple opposite the treasury, watching how the people cast in their offerings: and many that were rich cast in much. And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing. And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living. The narrative is one of the most theologically dense in the Gospels for its compactness, and several structural points emerge. First, Christ’s assessment overturns the human measurement: the rich gave more in absolute terms, but the widow gave more in proportion-to-what-she-had. The two mites, an objectively trivial sum, are by Christ’s reckoning more than the wealthy donors’ substantial gifts. Second, the measure of biblical giving is therefore not the absolute amount but the proportion-to-what-one-has and the degree-to-which-it-cost. The widow’s two mites cost her everything (all her living); the rich men’s much-larger gifts cost them very little (of their abundance). Third, the narrative is set as Christ’s explicit teaching to His disciples (and he called unto him his disciples): the lesson is meant for the church across the ages, not for the one moment. Fourth, the widow herself is anonymous, unrecognized in her own time, vindicated only by Christ’s seeing-and-naming her gift. The Gospel-narrator’s preserving of her example forever in Scripture is itself part of the lesson: what God sees and values, the world often does not—and the unnoticed widow of the temple-court is honored eternally in the canonical Word, while the wealthy donors of her day are nameless and forgotten. The mite-narrative therefore stands as a structural NT teaching on the nature of biblical giving: not measured in absolute amounts, judged by proportion and cost, valued by what is rendered in faith from what one actually has, seen by the Christ who knows the heart even when men do not see the gift.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MITE as a small particle; the smallest brass coin among the ancient Jews; equal to half a farthing; in scripture, the smallest copper coin in NT-era Palestine, the widow’s two mites being Christ’s exemplar of biblical giving measured by proportion and cost rather than absolute amount.

MITE, n. — 1. A small insect of the genus Acarus. 2. The smallest brass coin among the Jews, equal to half a farthing. And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing (Mark 12:42). 3. A particle; an atom; any thing very small.

FARTHING, n. — The fourth of a penny; a small copper coin of Britain. In the Bible, two mites made one farthing (Mark 12:42).

📖 Key Scripture

Mark 12:42-44 — "And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing. And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living."

Luke 21:1-4 — "And he looked up, and saw the rich men casting their gifts into the treasury. And he saw also a certain poor widow casting in thither two mites. And he said, Of a truth I say unto you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all: For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had."

2 Corinthians 8:12 — "For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."

Luke 12:59 — "I tell thee, thou shalt not depart thence, till thou hast paid the very last mite."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The widow’s mite is corrupted in contemporary use, on one side, by sentimentalized application that has reduced it to a feel-good story about humble giving without the structural challenge to the rich-giving-of-abundance pattern Christ explicitly criticized—and on the other by the prosperity-gospel pattern that asks the widow to give her last living as a seed-faith offering with the promise of a hundredfold return, against the narrative’s actual logic.

expand to see more

The sentimentalized application has reduced the widow’s mite to a feel-good story about humble giving, often emphasized in stewardship sermons to encourage modest givers without pressing the structural challenge to the comfortable-giving-of-abundance pattern Christ explicitly criticized. The narrative is sharper than the sentimentalization registers. Christ does not merely commend the widow; He criticizes the rich, by name and pattern: they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living. The contrast is not good for her, also good for them; the contrast is between giving-from-overflow (which costs the giver nothing) and giving-of-all-one-has (which costs the giver everything). The implied challenge to the comfortable believer is structural: am I giving from abundance (cheap to me, however much it may be in absolute terms) or in a way that costs me something? The recovery is the recovery of the narrative’s actual logic: biblical giving is measured by what the gift costs the giver, not by the absolute amount placed in the treasury.

The opposite corruption is the prosperity-gospel pattern that has read the widow’s mite as a model for the believer who is to give her last living as a seed-faith offering with the promise of a hundredfold material return. This grossly misreads the narrative. The widow gave her last living; there is no indication that she expected or received material return; she is commended for her sacrifice without any hint that the sacrifice was a transaction for greater material gain. The narrative is a tribute to costly giving without the prosperity-gospel transactional logic, and the contemporary teachers who solicit similar offerings from desperate widows with promises of return-on-investment are repeating a pattern that Christ explicitly criticized elsewhere: woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation (Matt 23:14). Recover both ends. Refuse the sentimentalization that removes the challenge, and refuse the prosperity-gospel reading that converts costly giving into transactional speculation. The widow’s mite stands as Christ’s permanent teaching on the nature of biblical giving: measured by cost-to-the-giver, valued by proportion-to-what-one-has, seen and honored by the Christ who sits opposite the treasury and watches what each soul actually gives.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek lepton (a thin one, the smallest copper coin in NT-era Palestine), rendered mite in the KJV; the coin of the widow’s two-mite offering that Christ commends as more than the rich men’s substantial gifts because measured by proportion-and-cost rather than absolute amount.

expand to see more

Greek lepton (G3016) — a thin one, the smallest copper coin (Mark 12:42; Luke 12:59; 21:2).

Greek kodrantēs (G2835) — quadrans, a small Roman copper (two mites; Mark 12:42, “which make a farthing”).

Greek dēnarion (G1220) — denarius, a single day’s wage for a laborer (Matt 20:2; the mite was approximately 1/256 of this).

Greek thēsauros (G2344) — treasury; here the temple treasury opposite which Christ sat watching the offerings (Mark 12:41).
